cards.def: A dramatic genre of humorously confusing, sometimes ridiculous situations that ends happily, often in one or more marriages.
A dramatic representation of the fall of kings or nobles, beginning in happiness and ending in catastrophe, the opposite of comedy.
A figure of thought that conjoins normally incompatible terms.
A work that uses the conventions of a particular genre in order to mock, comically, a topos, a genre, or a particular exponent of a genre.
A figure of thought that makes a sudden and sometimes ridiculous descent of tone.
A figure of thought that addresses an absent person, a force, or a quality.
A passing but illuminating reference within a literary text to another, well-known text, often biblical or classical.
A figure of thought in which a single word or expression has a sometimes irresolvable doubleness of meaning.
A feature of drama in which the audience knows that the outcome of an action will be the opposite of that intended by a character.
A genre that complains of contemporary ills, often with a first-person speaker, topical reference, and invective.
A costly court entertainment involving dance, song, speech, and elaborate stage effects, in which courtiers themselves participated.
The decisive turn in tragedy by which the plot is resolved and, usually, the protagonist dies.
The point at which a narrative can be resolved and so ended.
A topos in which the individual elements of a beloved's face and body are singled out for hyperbolic admiration.
The stylistic level of words, including their degree of formality, chosen according to audience and situation.
Unrhymed iambic pentameter lines, broken into verse paragraphs by sense rather than stanza form.
